first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this, so I'll read it all, top to bottom. The opening is calm and grown-up: "A Javanese wedding is not one ceremony. It is a sequence that can begin months before the day." Good. That tells me straight away this won't be one weekend, and I need to know that for flights and leave. But most of the page is about rituals. It isn't about who looks after us, and I'm the one paying for half of it.

journey.quote: Siraman, the cleansing bath, and midodareni, a quiet night of advice and prayer, both fall before the vow, so elders need to arrive early.
journey.reaction: Useful. That's exactly the kind of thing I'd miss. Mum would need extra nights, and that's extra accommodation I'll be paying for.

journey.quote: Australians marrying in Indonesia need the same recognised religion, a Certificate of No Impediment and the right registry, so check each step with the embassy and the registry.
journey.reaction: Straight to the point about the legal side, and they tell you to go to the embassy rather than pretending to be the authority. I trust that more than a glossy promise.

journey.section: What is a traditional Javanese wedding?
journey.quote: On its page about royal weddings, the Kraton Ngayogyakarta Hadiningrat states that in Javanese tradition the wedding is held by the bride's side.
journey.reaction: Hold on, the bride's side holds it? If that's us, what does 'holding it' mean in practice and in money? I'd be forwarding this line to my husband with a question mark.

journey.quote: In the palace account it is given by the bride's mother, the future mother-in-law and senior relatives as a blessing, with the bride bathed first and the couple at separate times and places.
journey.reaction: So I'd have a part in this myself. Nice to know, but nobody has told me what I'd actually do or wear.

journey.quote: For a destination wedding, plan two private bathing spaces and a gap in the run sheet so elders can move between them.
journey.reaction: This is the one sentence that thinks about older people moving around. I want much more of it: steps, distances, shade, somewhere to sit. My mother uses a walking frame.

journey.section: 9. Sungkeman: asking for the parents' blessing
journey.quote: In family weddings, the couple kneel before their elders.
journey.reaction: Lovely, and a bit emotional for me. But who's kneeling and who's sitting matters when the grandparents can't get up and down easily. Again, nothing practical.

journey.quote: A 2026 study in the journal DESILLES examines truntum worn by parents on the wedding day.
journey.reaction: I don't need journal names. Tell me if I'm expected to wear a particular batik and where I'd get one. That's the part that's actually about me, and it's buried.

journey.quote: It is often told that the groom's family brings cloth, a ring and foods on trays; what goes in is a conversation for the two families rather than a stylist.
journey.reaction: "It is often told" comes up again and again. I can see they're being careful, but by the fifth time it feels like nobody really knows.

journey.section: Can Australians legally marry in Java or Bali?
journey.quote: Under Indonesian Law No. 1 of 1974, both partners must hold the same religion, or one must convert.
journey.reaction: That's a big one for our family, and I'm glad it's said plainly rather than hidden. It's a conversation I'd need to have with my daughter before anyone pays a deposit.

journey.section: Can Australians legally marry in Java or Bali?
journey.quote: Smartraveller also notes that the revised criminal code includes penalties for cohabitation and sex outside marriage.
journey.reaction: That gave me a fright, and then the page just moves on. Does it affect an engaged couple sharing a room, or our guests? One sentence of explanation, or a pointer to where to check, would settle my nerves.

journey.section: Can Australians legally marry in Java or Bali?
journey.quote: Its volcano list includes Mount Merapi, between Central Java and Yogyakarta, and Mount Semeru in East Java. Keep a weather and transfer Plan B for outdoor rites.
journey.reaction: Good that they're honest about it. But 'keep a Plan B' is advice to me. I want to know who makes and runs that Plan B, and what happens to the money if flights are cancelled.

journey.section: Planning a Javanese wedding with both families
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor is your single point of contact for everything around them, with the fee and inclusions agreed in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: This is the sentence I was waiting for, and it comes at the very end. One person, and the fee in writing. I'd like it much earlier, and I'd like to know I can speak to them on the phone.

unanswered_questions: If something goes wrong in Yogyakarta at 2am, who do I ring, and are they in Australia or Indonesia?
Are deposits paid to Indonesian suppliers protected, and is the contract in English and in AUD?
Can my mother, who uses a walking frame, manage a traditional house, a pendopo or the venues these rites use? Is there accessible transport from the airport?
What travel and medical insurance should older guests have, and how far are the nearest good hospitals from Yogyakarta or Solo?
If 'the wedding is held by the bride's side', what does that mean for the bride's parents' costs and responsibilities?
Is the mother of the bride expected to wear particular batik, and who arranges it?
Does the cohabitation part of the criminal code affect an engaged couple or guests sharing rooms?
Can I have a phone call with a Wedded Advisor before anything is booked?

turn_offs_found.quote: No mention of deposits, supplier contracts or who is responsible if a supplier fails, apart from: "with the fee and inclusions agreed in writing before you commit."
turn_offs_found.why: Deposits and accountability are my main worry about overseas suppliers. The page covers the advisor's own fee but says nothing about protecting the money we pay to suppliers in Indonesia.

turn_offs_found.quote: The Australian Embassy says neither DFAT nor its missions can advise on another country's marriage requirements; contact the Indonesian Embassy or the Civil Registry Office where you will marry, and consider a lawyer in Australia or Indonesia. Persons of any nationality may generally marry in Indonesia if they hold a religion the Indonesian Government recognises, and the marriage must follow that religion. Under Indonesian Law No. 1 of 1974, both partners must hold the same religion, or one must convert.
turn_offs_found.why: This legal section is a wall of text on an iPad. It's the part I most need to read carefully and pass to my husband, so short steps or a checklist would help a lot.

would_share_with: My husband, with the legal section and the 'bride's side' line marked
My daughter, to ask which of these steps the groom's family actually expects

cta_reaction.quote: If you are weighing Java, Bali or a wedding at home, Wedded Concierge is a good place to begin that conversation.
cta_reaction.why: The fee in writing and one point of contact are the right things to say. But 'begin that conversation' doesn't tell me whether I'll get a real person on the phone or a form, and the page never says what the advisor actually does about suppliers, deposits or elderly guests on the day. I'd click if it said I could book a call.

top_3_changes: Bring the Wedded Advisor promise (one point of contact, fee in writing) up earlier, and say plainly what the advisor handles: supplier contracts, deposits, and who to call if something goes wrong on the day, plus that a phone call comes before anything is booked.

Add a short practical section for families travelling with elders: extra nights for siraman and midodareni, accessibility of homes and pendopo, transfers, travel and medical insurance, and what parents of the bride are expected to do and wear.
Break the legal section into short numbered steps, and add one line explaining what the criminal code note means (or where to check) for engaged couples and guests, so it informs rather than alarms.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction has an exact quote from the draft (turn-off 1 quotes the only related sentence and notes the absence)
Stayed in character as Margaret, mother of the bride paying about half, reading on an iPad from a link her daughter sent
No invented brand facts; things the page does not say are listed in unanswered_questions
HTML comments, fact markers and image slots treated as invisible
Missing prices and deferred business details not raised as must-fix, per orchestrator instruction

open_questions.question: Persona is provisional and uncalibrated (weight 0.20). Should the elder-travel and deposit-protection gaps be weighed as content gaps for this cultural guide, or deferred to the CRO and business-detail stages?
Is there an approved, sourced line on what the Wedded Advisor does about supplier deposits and on-the-day emergencies that could move earlier in the post?

assumptions: Margaret's daughter is planning, or considering, a Javanese wedding in Indonesia, so the destination, legal and elder-travel content is relevant to her.
Read on an iPad, top to bottom, per decision_behaviour.
Absence of prices and business details is expected at this stage and not penalised as must-fix.
